title: Inside Cloudflare Pages: A System Design Deep Dive
partialText:
Every time you run git push to deploy a frontend application, a deceptive amount of engineering is hidden behind that green checkmark. Within seconds, your code is built, hashed, distributed across hundreds of edge locations worldwide, and made accessible at a custom URL with zero cold starts.

For years, the Jamstack and static site hosting ecosystem (AWS S3 + CloudFront, Netlify, Vercel) relied on a conventional architecture: compile assets in a centralized cloud runner, upload blobs to centralized object storage (like AWS S3 in us-east-1), invalidate a CDN cache, and spin up containerized serverless functions in regional datacenters for dynamic routes.

Cloudflare Pages took an entirely different architectural route. Instead of treating the edge as a caching proxy in front of central origins, Cloudflare built Pages natively inside its global Anycast network, treating static asset hosting as an edge-native compute problem.

This post breaks down the architecture, internal source code mechanics, and distributed systems engineering that power Cloudflare Pages: from gVisor container isolation and content-addressable storage to binary-searchable manifests and O(1) dynamic dispatch.

Part 1: The World Before Cloudflare Pages

How Traditional Edge Hosting Worked

Before edge-native platforms emerged, hosting a modern frontend application (React, Vue, Next.js, Hugo, Astro) followed a standardized, multi-tier pattern:

  1. Build Step: A CI runner boots a generic VM or Docker container, clones the repository, runs npm run build, and generates static output files.
  2. Central Ingestion: The runner syncs files to a centralized bucket (e.g., AWS S3 in us-east-1).
  3. Cache Purging: The deployment triggers a global CDN cache invalidation via API.
  4. Edge Fetch on Miss: When a user in Singapore or London visits the site, the local edge CDN suffers a cache miss, traverses transit links back to us-east-1 to pull the asset, and caches it locally with a TTL.
  5. Serverless Functions: If dynamic server-side rendering (SSR) or API routes are needed, the request is forwarded to AWS Lambda or regional container instances.

The Three Structural Flaws of This Model

  1. The Origin Round-Trip Penalty (Cache Miss Latency)
    CDNs are historically dumb caches sitting in front of smart, centralized origins. A cold request from Tokyo to an origin in Virginia incurs ~150–200ms of raw round-trip time (RTT) alone, before TLS negotiation, server processing, and asset streaming even begin.
  2. The Cache Invalidation & Consistency Nightmare
    “There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.” Centralized CDNs rely on TTLs or eventual-consistency cache purge queues. During a deployment rollover, clients frequently experience race conditions: fetching new index.html referencing old chunk hashes, or vice versa, resulting in broken JavaScript bundles and runtime crashes.
  3. Cold Starts and Container Latency
    Dynamic API routes deployed to traditional serverless runtimes (AWS Lambda, Google Cloud Run) require container spin-up time — often adding 250ms to 2+ seconds of latency on cold hits.

Part 2: The System Design of Cloudflare Pages

Design Goals

  1. Zero Origin Dependency: Assets must live directly on the edge network; no origin server to traverse.
  2. Instant, Atomic Deployments: Rollouts must be atomic, instant, and immune to stale-cache skew.
  3. Sub-Millisecond Routing Overhead: Edge dispatch must not degrade as projects scale from 1 deployment to 50,000 deployments.
  4. Unified Compute & Asset Pipeline: Static assets and serverless execution must share the same runtime context.

High-Level System Architecture

Part 3: Deep Technical Mechanisms (Under the Hood)

1. Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) and Delta Deployments

When you push a build using Wrangler CLI or Pages CI, Cloudflare does not upload a zip archive or blindly overwrite remote files. Instead, Pages uses a Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) architecture.

Step 1: Client-Side Content Hashing

The local CLI or build runner scans the build output directory and computes a 32-character hex hash for every file using SHA-256 over its base64 content and extension:

// Extracted from Cloudflare Wrangler asset pipeline
const fileContent = fs.readFileSync(fullPath);
const extension = extname(relativePath).substring(1);
const hash = crypto
  .createHash("sha256")
  .update(fileContent.toString("base64") + extension)
  .digest("hex")
  .slice(0, 32);
manifest[manifestPath] = { hash, size: fileContent.length };

Step 2: Global Deduplication Query (/pages/assets/check-missing)

Before transferring a single byte of payload, Wrangler sends all hashes to Cloudflare’s control plane:

POST /pages/assets/check-missing
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
{
  "hashes": ["7a9f2b...", "d41d8c...", "3e8821..."]
}

Cloudflare checks its global storage index. If an asset hash already exists — whether from a previous commit in the same repo or an identical vendor library (react.production.min.js) uploaded by another build—it returns only the missing hashes.

In real-world web apps where only a few CSS/JS bundles change per commit, up to 95% of assets are deduplicated instantly.

Step 3: Concurrent Chunked Uploads

The missing files are packed into buckets (maximum 50 MiB per bucket) and uploaded concurrently over HTTP using a bounded concurrency queue (PQueue with concurrency = 3):

const payload = bucket.files.map((file) => ({
  key: file.hash,
  value: readFile(file.path).toString("base64"),
  metadata: { contentType: file.contentType },
  base64: true
}));
await fetchResult("/pages/assets/upload", {
  method: "POST",
  body: JSON.stringify(payload)
});

Because files are keyed by content hash, assets are strictly immutable. Storing an asset with a hash 7a9f2b... means it will never change.

2. The Binary-Searchable Manifest: O(\log n) Edge Memory Lookup

Traditional static hosting platforms store project file listings in a giant JSON manifest or SQL database. In early iterations of serverless static sites, reading and parsing a 20,000-file JSON manifest at runtime caused massive GC pauses, high memory consumption, and 100ms+ parsing latency inside the edge runtime.

Cloudflare solved this inside @cloudflare/workers-shared/asset-worker by compiling the manifest into a raw binary byte buffer (ArrayBuffer / Uint8Array):

Every route path is hashed with SHA-256 to a fixed byte length (PATH_HASH_SIZE). Entries in the binary buffer are sorted lexicographically by pathHash.

When an HTTP request arrives:

// Extracted from @cloudflare/workers-shared/asset-worker/src/assets-manifest.ts
export class AssetsManifest {
  private data: Uint8Array;
constructor(data: ArrayBuffer) {
    this.data = new Uint8Array(data);
  }
  async get(pathname: string) {
    const pathHash = await hashPath(pathname);
    const entry = binarySearch(this.data, pathHash);
    return entry ? Uint8ToHexString(entry) : null;
  }
}

The binarySearch function operates directly on the raw memory buffer using bitwise division:

export const binarySearch = (
  manifest: Uint8Array,
  pathHash: Uint8Array
): Uint8Array | false => {
  const numberOfEntries = (manifest.byteLength - HEADER_SIZE) / ENTRY_SIZE;
  let lowIndex = 0;
  let highIndex = numberOfEntries - 1;
  while (lowIndex <= highIndex) {
    const middleIndex = (lowIndex + highIndex) >> 1;
    const cmp = comparePathHashWithEntry(pathHash, manifest, middleIndex);
    if (cmp < 0) {
      highIndex = middleIndex - 1;
      continue;
    }
    if (cmp > 0) {
      lowIndex = middleIndex + 1;
      continue;
    }
// Exact Match: extract the Content Hash (ETag) directly from buffer offset
    return new Uint8Array(
      manifest.buffer,
      HEADER_SIZE + middleIndex * ENTRY_SIZE + CONTENT_HASH_OFFSET,
      CONTENT_HASH_SIZE
    );
  }
  return false;
};

Why This Engineering Detail Matters:

  • Zero JSON Parsing: No string serialization or JSON deserialization.
  • Zero V8 Garbage Collection Pressure: Searching across 20,000 routes generates no object allocations.
  • Microsecond Lookups: Binary search across a sorted byte slice takes O(\log n) CPU cycles — completing in under 5 microseconds.

Once the content hash (ETag) is retrieved:

  1. If the client sent If-None-Match: "<content-hash>", the Asset Worker immediately returns 304 Not Modified without fetching the payload from storage.
  2. If the payload is needed, it fetches the stream from KV with an aggressive 1-year edge cache TTL:
// Extracted from @cloudflare/workers-shared/asset-worker/src/utils/kv.ts
const asset = await assetsKVNamespace.getWithMetadata<AssetMetadata>(
  assetKey, // Content Hash
  {
    type: "stream",
    cacheTtl: 31536000 // 1 year! Safe because content is immutable
  }
);

3. From O(n) Regex Routing to O(1) Dynamic Dispatch

As Cloudflare Pages gained adoption, engineering teams created thousands of preview deployments per project (one for every git branch and commit).

The Bottleneck:

Originally, every Pages project stored a routing table in Quicksilver (Cloudflare’s globally replicated in-memory key-value store). The routing table was a JSON array of regex rules mapping request hostnames and paths to deployment pipelines.

For projects with 10,000 to 50,000 preview deployments, this JSON routing table ballooned to several megabytes:

  • On every request, the edge node downloaded the JSON from Quicksilver.
  • Parsed the multi-megabyte JSON in memory.
  • Iterated sequentially through thousands of regular expressions (O(n) scan).

In production, median lookup latency climbed to 136ms, and large projects saw multi-second delays just to decide which pipeline to run!

The Fix: Workers for Platforms Dynamic Dispatch

Cloudflare redesigned the routing tier by adopting Workers for Platforms (dynamic dispatch namespaces).

Instead of storing regex rules, Cloudflare calculates a deterministic cryptographic hash of the deployment hostname with a cluster secret at deployment time:

      Pipeline ID = HMAC-SHA256(hostname, Secret)

Results of This Architectural Migration (14 Million Deployments):

  • Lookup Latency: Reduced from 136ms+ to < 1ms (O(1) constant time).
  • Edge Storage: Reduced Quicksilver storage by 92% (~12 GiB freed per PoP).
  • CPU & LRU Hit Rate: Prevented single large routing tables from evicting other cache entries in edge memory.

4. Fast & Secure Build Isolation: gVisor Sandboxes

A developer platform is only as good as its build pipeline. During the initial rollout of Pages, build runners created a full virtual machine (VM) for each git commit.

  • The Problem: Booting a clean VM, mounting storage, and initializing build dependencies took 2+ minutes before the user’s npm run build even executed.
  • The Dilemma: Standard Docker/container reuse was fast, but containers share the host Linux kernel. In a multi-tenant environment executing untrusted user build scripts, a kernel exploit would enable container breakouts.

The Solution: Warm VM Pools + gVisor Sandboxing

Cloudflare transitioned to gVisor — an open-source, user-space kernel developed by Google.

  • Each Pages container runs with its own isolated application kernel implemented in Go, intercepting system calls and eliminating raw access to the host kernel.
  • Cloudflare maintains a pool of pre-warmed virtual machines across its compute clusters.
  • When a git webhook triggers a build, a gVisor sandbox boots in 2 to 3 seconds (a 98% reduction in initialization latency).
  • Build logs are multiplexed and streamed in real time over WebSockets to the developer dashboard.

Part 4: Unified Execution Pipeline (Assets + Functions)

Frontend architecture has shifted from purely static SPAs to hybrid, full-stack frameworks (Remix, Next.js, SvelteKit, Astro). Pages addresses this by unifying static assets and serverless functions into a single pipeline composed of specialized Workers:

Static vs. Dynamic Routing Rules (_routes.json)

To prevent billing developers for static asset requests, Pages automatically generates or evaluates a _routes.json file:

{
  "version": 1,
  "include": ["/*"],
  "exclude": ["/build/*", "/assets/*", "/favicon.ico"]
}
  1. Rule Evaluation:
    - The Router Worker matches the incoming path against exclude rules first.
    - If excluded, the request is forwarded directly to the Asset Server Worker (free, unlimited requests).
    - If included, it dispatches to the User Worker (V8 Isolate executing Pages Functions).
  2. The env.ASSETS Binding:
    Even when the User Worker handles the request (e.g., for authentication middleware or SSR), it receives an internal env.ASSETS binding. It can programmatically invoke env.ASSETS.fetch(request) to fetch static assets from the co-located Asset Worker without extra network hops.

Part 5: Complete Request Lifecycle Trace

Let’s trace what happens when a user requests https://my-app.pages.dev/dashboard:

  1. Anycast Routing & TLS Termination: The browser establishes an HTTP/3 connection with the topologically closest Cloudflare edge node (sub-10ms latency).
  2. Dynamic Pipeline Resolution: Pingora passes the request to the dynamic dispatch layer. The hostname my-app.pages.dev is hashed to locate the pipeline in O(1) time.
  3. Route & Header Evaluation: The Asset Worker evaluates _redirects and _headers.
  4. Binary Manifest Probe: The path /dashboard is hashed with SHA-256. A binary search runs across the in-memory array buffer in < 5\mu\text{s}. If /dashboard.html exists, its 32-character content hash is extracted.
  5. Conditional Cache Validation:
    - If not, the Worker fetches the stream from edge KV storage / Tiered Cache with a 1-year TTL.
    - If the request has an If-None-Match header matching the content hash, the Worker immediately responds with 304 Not Modified.
  6. Zero-Copy Streaming Response: The asset is streamed to the client with full HTTP caching headers.

Total time elapsed at the edge: < 15ms.

Part 6: The Strategic Layer — Why Cloudflare Built Pages

Nothing Cloudflare builds exists in a vacuum. Pages was a calculated move to dominate the developer platform market:

  1. Marginal Bandwidth and Compute Cost ≈ Zero
    Cloudflare operates a global Anycast network for its primary CDN, DDoS, and WAF businesses. Every server in every PoP already runs the full Cloudflare software stack. Serving a few kilobytes of HTML and JavaScript from an existing server incurs negligible marginal cost compared to cloud providers who lease transit and compute.
  2. The Gateway Drug to Cloudflare Workers and Developer Storage
    Static site hosting is a commoditized entry point. Once developers host their frontend on Pages, they naturally adopt Pages Functions, which require Workers KV, Cloudflare D1 (SQL), Cloudflare R2 (Object Storage), and Workers AI. Pages is the acquisition funnel for Cloudflare’s multi-billion-dollar developer ecosystem.
  3. Unification into Workers Static Assets
    Pages proved that static asset hosting is simply a specialized Worker binding. In 2024–2025, Cloudflare completed the circle by bringing Pages’ asset architecture directly into core Cloudflare Workers via [assets] bindings, allowing any Worker to host static files with zero architectural friction.

Key Takeaways for System Designers

  1. Immutability Enables Aggressive Caching
    By keying assets to SHA-256 content hashes, Cloudflare eliminated cache invalidation entirely. Blobs can be safely cached for 1 year (cacheTtl: 31536000) without stale-asset bugs.
  2. Data Structure Choice Dictates Latency
    Switching from a JSON string manifest to a sorted binary byte buffer transformed route resolution from a high-GC, multi-millisecond operation into a 5-microsecond O(\log n) memory search.
  3. Eliminate Multi-Step Indirection at Scale
    Transitioning from an O(n) regex routing table in Quicksilver to an O(1) secret hash dispatch in Workers for Platforms eliminated 136ms of overhead across 14 million deployments.
  4. Sandboxing Doesn’t Have to Mean Slow Boot Times
    Pre-warmed pools of VMs running gVisor provide true kernel-level multi-tenant isolation with container-level startup speeds (2 seconds vs 2 minutes).
  5. Co-Locate Everything on the Edge
    When your DNS, routing, compute runtime, and asset store live on the exact same machine in 330+ cities worldwide, origin round trips cease to exist.

Sources & Further Reading:

  • Cloudflare Blog: “Making Cloudflare Pages the fastest way to serve your sites” (2023)
  • Cloudflare Blog: “A new era for Cloudflare Pages builds” (2022)
  • Cloudflare Open Source: @cloudflare/workers-sdk (packages/workers-shared/asset-worker)
  • Cloudflare Documentation: “Static Assets and Routing Architecture”

Inside Cloudflare Pages: A System Design Deep Dive was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Version Hunting: From Server Banner to CVE in 3 Steps
partialText:
A version string means nothing until you run it through a pipeline. Here is the pipeline.

Series: curl — The Request Engine You Never Learned Properly Article: 9 of 16

Article 4 taught you to read response headers and build a technology profile. This article teaches you what to do with it.

The gap between “I found Apache 2.4.49” and “I have a path traversal vulnerability” is not skill — it is methodology. A structured pipeline: extract the version, assess your confidence in it, search for CVEs, filter the results, and verify before claiming. Three steps, repeatable, documented.

Starting from Your Header Catalogue

In Article 4, you built the habit of running:

curl -sI http://target.com

Read the response headers for version strings. From this response:

Server: Apache/2.4.49 (Ubuntu)
X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3

You have two version strings to work with: Apache 2.4.49 and PHP 7.4.3. Before running any searches, assess what you actually know.

The Confidence Rating Table

Version information from headers is not equally reliable. Treating an inferred version the same as an exact version confirmed from a banner leads to false positives — and false positives waste time and damage credibility in real reports.

Use this table before every CVE search:

Tier  Evidence                          Confidence  Report language
----  --------------------------------  ----------  ------------------------------------------
1     Server: Apache/2.4.49             High        "Version 2.4.49 confirmed via Server header"
2     Server: Apache/2.4.x (partial)    Medium      "Version in the 2.4.x range, exact build unknown"
3     Server: Apache (no version)       Low         "Apache detected; version not disclosed"
4     Inferred from behavior            Low         "Consistent with Apache behavior; not confirmed"
5     No banner, generic headers        None        "Server technology not determined"

Applying the table:

Server: Apache/2.4.49 → Tier 1. You have the exact version. CVE searches will be precise. Note that Tier 1 means the banner is exact — it does not guarantee the version is unpatched. Distribution maintainers backport fixes without changing the version string. Tier 1 tells you where to search; behavioral verification tells you whether it is actually exploitable.

X-Powered-By: PHP/7.4.3 → Tier 1. Exact PHP version disclosed.

Server: nginx (no version) → Tier 3. You know it is nginx, not which version. CVE searches will return everything affecting nginx — broad and mostly not actionable without narrowing.

Set-Cookie: PHPSESSID=... with no X-Powered-By → Tier 4. PHP is running, version unknown. Note it; do not claim a specific version.

This table goes into your notes. In a real report, the confidence tier determines how you phrase findings. A Tier 1 finding is stated as fact. A Tier 4 finding is stated as an inference.

Step 1: Extract Version Strings

The manual method you already know. For automation across multiple endpoints, narrow the output to only version-bearing headers:

curl -sI http://10.49.179.59 | grep -iE "server|x-powered-by|x-generator|x-aspnet|x-runtime"
Server: Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)

One line. Tier 1 immediately — exact version, OS, distribution. That version string is the input for every search that follows.

Run the same filter against a different target, and you get a different stack:

curl -sI http://10.38.1.120:4280 | grep -iE "server|x-powered-by|x-generator|x-aspnet|x-runtime"
Server: Apache/2.4.67 (Debian)
X-Powered-By: PHP/8.5.6

Two version strings from one command. Both Tier 1. Both searchable.

For internet-facing targets, the header can reveal a completely different stack:

curl -sI https://httpbin.org/get | grep -iE "server|x-powered-by|x-generator|x-aspnet|x-runtime"
server: gunicorn/19.9.0

Python WSGI server, exact version. Same command, different signal.

Saving for later processing:

# Log IP and status code
curl -sI http://10.49.179.59 \
  -o /dev/null \
  -w "%{remote_ip} %{http_code}\n" \
  2>/dev/null >> ip_log.txt
cat ip_log.txt
10.49.179.59 200

Timestamped evidence capture:

curl -sI http://10.49.179.59 | tee -a "$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_headers.txt"
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sun, 31 May 2026 11:35:32 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)
Last-Modified: Sat, 17 Aug 2019 16:03:12 GMT
ETag: "2c39-590523e6dfcd7"
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Content-Length: 11321
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Content-Type: text/html

tee -a appends to the file while still printing to stdout. The timestamp in the filename tells you exactly when the evidence was captured — critical for reports and for correlating findings across a session. The file writes to your current working directory; if you are sweeping multiple targets, use a dedicated subdirectory to keep output organized.

Sweeping multiple targets:

echo "10.49.179.59" > targets.txt
while read host; do
  echo "=== $host ===" >> headers.txt
  curl -sI --max-time 5 "http://$host" | grep -iE "server|x-powered-by|x-generator" >> headers.txt
done < targets.txt
cat headers.txt
=== 10.49.179.59 ===
Server: Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)

--max-time 5 prevents the loop from stalling on slow or unresponsive hosts. In a network range sweep, one host with no response can hang the loop for its full timeout — without this flag, that compounds across every dead host in your list. Note that five seconds may also cut off slow but genuinely responsive hosts; adjust based on network conditions. Scale to a full subnet list, and you have a version catalogue across an entire engagement scope in minutes.

Step 2: CVE Hunting Pipeline

With a confirmed version, run three searches in sequence.

Search 1 — NVD (National Vulnerability Database):

https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/search

Search: Apache 2.4.49

NVD gives you authoritative CVE entries with CVSS scores, affected version ranges, and references. For Apache 2.4.49, CVE-2021–41773 (path traversal / RCE) appears prominently. CVSS 9.8 applies when mod_cgi is enabled, and remote code execution is achievable; the path traversal alone scores lower. Read the affected version range — it tells you whether your exact version is in scope before you write a single word in your notes.

Search 2 — ExploitDB via searchsploit:

searchsploit apache 2.4.49
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------
 Exploit Title                                                            |  Path
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------
Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49 - Path Traversal & Remote Code Execution (RCE) | multiple/webapps/50383.sh
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------

ExploitDB gives you public exploits — not just vulnerability advisories. The difference matters: NVD tells you a vulnerability exists; ExploitDB tells you working exploit code is publicly available. A CVE with a public exploit raises the priority immediately. No research required to weaponize it — someone already did.

The title says path traversal and RCE. The path traversal works without mod_cgi; the RCE escalation requires it. The exploit script covers both paths, but the achievable severity depends entirely on whether mod_cgi is enabled on the target.

Search 3 — Broader version range:

searchsploit apache 2.4
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------
 Exploit Title                                                            |  Path
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------
Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49 - Path Traversal & Remote Code Execution (RCE) | multiple/webapps/50383.sh
Apache HTTP Server 2.4.50 - Path Traversal & Remote Code Execution (RCE) | multiple/webapps/50406.sh
Apache HTTP Server 2.4.50 - Remote Code Execution (RCE) (2)              | multiple/webapps/50446.sh
Apache HTTP Server 2.4.50 - Remote Code Execution (RCE) (3)              | multiple/webapps/50512.py
Apache 2.4.17 < 2.4.38 - 'apache2ctl graceful' 'logrotate' Local Privilege Escalation | linux/local/46676.php
Apache 2.4.x - Buffer Overflow                                            | multiple/webapps/51193.py
[... additional results ...]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------

Search the major version range too. Vulnerabilities affecting the 2.4.x branch may not list every minor version — a broader search catches entries that an exact-version search misses.

Search PHP separately:

searchsploit php 7.4

The results include noise from unrelated products whose version strings happen to contain 7.4 — searchsploit matches on the full title string, so anything versioned 7.4 appears regardless of product. When the output is a wall of results, filter harder. Search PHP 7.4 FFI or PHP 7.4 disable_functions to surface the actual PHP engine vulnerabilities. Two entries in that output are genuine PHP 7.4 findings:

PHP 7.0 < 7.4 (Unix) - 'debug_backtrace' disable_functions Bypass | php/local/48072.php
PHP 7.4 FFI - 'disable_functions' Bypass                          | php/webapps/48655.php

Both are disable_functions bypasses — relevant if you land in a restricted PHP environment and need to break out.

Step 3: False Positive Filtering

This is the step most beginners skip. Finding a CVE that affects your version range does not mean the target is exploitable. Before claiming a finding, filter it through four checks.

Check 1 — Exact version confirmed:

CVE-2021–41773 affects Apache 2.4.49 specifically. Not 2.4.48. Not 2.4.50. The initial patch shipped in 2.4.50, but it was incomplete — CVE-2021–42013 affects both 2.4.49 and 2.4.50. The full fix did not land until 2.4.51. Version precision matters throughout this chain. Confirm Tier 1 before proceeding.

Check 2 — Version in affected range per CVE advisory:

Read the NVD entry, not just the title. The affected version range is explicit. Some CVEs cover a range (>= 2.4.17, < 2.4.38). If your target falls outside that range, the CVE does not apply regardless of how similar the version looks.

Check 3 — Vulnerable feature or module enabled:

CVE-2021–41773 requires mod_cgi to be enabled for RCE. The path traversal works without it, but command execution requires the module. You cannot determine this from headers alone — it requires probing:

# Common path traversal test — ethical lab environment only
# Exact path may vary by target configuration; /icons/ and other directories also work
curl -s "http://target.com/cgi-bin/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/etc/passwd"

A 200 response with /etc/passwd content confirms traversal. A 400 or 403 suggests the module is absent or the path is blocked. Neither is definitive without testing the actual execution path.

Check 4 — Patch status:

Linux distribution maintainers often backport patches and re-release with the same version string. A Debian or Ubuntu system showing Apache/2.4.49 may have CVE-2021-41773 patched at the OS level while the version string is unchanged. The only reliable verification is behavioral — probe the vulnerability directly in a legal context.

The false positive filter checklist:

[ ] Tier 1 confidence — exact version confirmed?
[ ] Version falls within affected range per CVE advisory?
[ ] Vulnerable feature or module confirmed enabled?
[ ] Behavioral verification passes?

Only after all four passes is a finding reportable as confirmed.

Nuclei Integration

Nuclei is a template-based scanner. Once curl gives you the version signal, Nuclei runs structured checks against it automatically.

# Technology detection templates
nuclei -u http://10.49.179.59 -t http/technologies/ -silent
[waf-detect:apachegeneric] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59
[apache-detect] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59 ["Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)"]
[default-apache-test-all] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59 ["Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)"]
[default-apache2-ubuntu-page] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59

Nuclei confirms what curl found: Apache 2.4.18 on Ubuntu, WAF detection firing on the generic Apache signature. No new information yet — this is corroboration.

# CVE templates — checks for known CVEs matching the target
nuclei -u http://10.49.179.59 -t http/cves/ -silent

No output. The CVE templates found nothing exploitable against Apache 2.4.18 via HTTP. That is useful information — it narrows the attack surface and tells you the web service is not the priority.

# Automatic scan — wappalyzer-based technology detection, broader coverage
nuclei -u http://10.49.179.59 -as -silent
[apache-detect] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59 ["Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)"]
[default-apache2-ubuntu-page] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59
[waf-detect:apachegeneric] [http] [info] http://10.49.179.59
[ftp-detect] [tcp] [info] 10.49.179.59:21
[vsftpd-detect:version] [tcp] [info] 10.49.179.59:21 ["3.0.3"]
[ftp-anonymous-login] [tcp] [medium] 10.49.179.59:21
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="123456",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="password",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="nas",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="pass1",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="stingray",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="toor",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="default",username="ftp"]
[ftp-weak-credentials] [tcp] [high] 10.49.179.59:21 [password="guest",username="ftp"]

This is the value of -as. The curl banner grab was looking at port 80. Nuclei's automatic scan expanded to TCP and found an FTP service on port 21 running vsftpd 3.0.3. It detected an anonymous login and reported weak credential patterns against the ftp account. These are Nuclei's detections — verify each credential interactively before treating any as confirmed valid. None of that came from the HTTP banner.

The curl signal pointed at the web service. Nuclei found a second attack surface that the banner grab missed entirely.

The integration workflow: curl for fast, precise, targeted identification — one command, one version string, immediate pivot to CVE search. Nuclei for automated template-based verification and broader surface coverage. They are not redundant; they are sequential.

Documenting as You Go

The best time to document a finding is immediately, not when you are writing the report hours later.

# Timestamped capture of the headers
curl -sI http://target.com | tee -a "$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_headers.txt"
# Capture the full response with timing
curl -v http://target.com -o "$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_response.txt" 2>&1

Minimum viable finding format:

Finding:      Apache Path Traversal
CVE:          CVE-2021-41773
Evidence:     Server: Apache/2.4.49 (Tier 1 — exact version banner)
Verification: curl -s "http://target.com/cgi-bin/.%2e/etc/passwd" returned file contents
Severity:     CVSS 9.8 with mod_cgi enabled (RCE) / lower for path traversal alone

Evidence type, verification method, severity with context. That format is what separates a note from a finding. Build it at the time of discovery — the command you just ran, the output you just saw, the confidence tier you just assigned.

Complete Walkthrough: Banner to CVE on Simple CTF

Target: TryHackMe Simple CTF (10.49.179.59). Full pipeline, annotated at each step.

Step 1 — Extract the banner:

curl -sI http://10.49.179.59 | grep -i server
Server: Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)

Tier 1 immediately. Exact version, OS, distribution. One command.

Step 2 — Full header dump for the record:

curl -sI http://10.49.179.59
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Date: Sun, 31 May 2026 11:34:15 GMT
Server: Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu)
Last-Modified: Sat, 17 Aug 2019 16:03:12 GMT
ETag: "2c39-590523e6dfcd7"
Accept-Ranges: bytes
Content-Length: 11321
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Content-Type: text/html

No X-Powered-By. No framework headers. Clean the Apache default page. Last-Modified: Sat, 17 Aug 2019 — The default page has not changed since 2019. Likely untouched since deployment.

Step 3 — CVE search:

searchsploit apache 2.4.18
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------
 Exploit Title                                                            |  Path
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------
Apache < 2.2.34 / < 2.4.27 - OPTIONS Memory Leak                         | linux/webapps/42745.py
Apache 2.4.17 < 2.4.38 - 'apache2ctl graceful' 'logrotate' LPE           | linux/local/46676.php
Apache mod_ssl < 2.8.7 OpenSSL - 'OpenFuck.c' Remote Buffer Overflow      | unix/remote/21671.c
[... additional results ...]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------- ---------------------------------

Two entries are directly relevant to 2.4.18:

Apache < 2.2.34 / < 2.4.27 - OPTIONS Memory Leak — 2.4.18 is below 2.4.27, so it falls in the affected range. Information disclosure via the OPTIONS method.

Apache 2.4.17 < 2.4.38 - 'apache2ctl graceful' 'logrotate' Local Privilege Escalation — 2.4.18 falls within the affected range. This is a local privilege escalation requiring existing authenticated access to the system. Not an initial access vector — a post-foothold escalation path worth noting.

The rest are version range mismatches or product mismatches (Tomcat, OpenMeetings, mod_ssl). Filter by reading the version range in the title, not just the product name.

Step 4 — Confidence tier and finding format:

Finding:      Apache Local Privilege Escalation
CVE:          CVE-2019-0211
Evidence:     Server: Apache/2.4.18 (Ubuntu) — Tier 1, exact version confirmed
Version range: Affects 2.4.17 through 2.4.37 — 2.4.18 is in range
Vector:       Local — requires existing authenticated access to the system
Severity:     High (post-exploitation escalation path)
Next step:    Verify logrotate configuration and apache2ctl access after foothold

Step 5 — Nuclei automatic scan:

nuclei -u http://10.49.179.59 -as -silent

The HTTP surface returned only informational findings — Apache version confirmed, default page detected. The automatic scan expanded to TCP and detected vsftpd 3.0.3 on port 21, reported anonymous login, and flagged weak credential patterns. Verify those interactively before treating any as confirmed.

That is the initial access surface. The Apache version gives you the post-exploitation path. Two tools, two different signals, one complete picture.

Version strings are not data points to collect and forget. They are the first link in a chain. Confidence rating before searching. Search before claiming. Verify before reporting. The chain is the methodology.

Quick Reference

EXTRACT VERSION STRINGS
curl -sI http://target | grep -iE "server|x-powered-by|x-generator|x-aspnet|x-runtime"
SAVE EVIDENCE
curl -sI http://target | tee -a "$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M%S)_headers.txt"
curl -sI http://target -o /dev/null -w "%{remote_ip} %{http_code}\n" >> ip_log.txt
SWEEP MULTIPLE TARGETS
while read host; do
  echo "=== $host ===" >> headers.txt
  curl -sI --max-time 5 "http://$host" | grep -iE "server|x-powered-by|x-generator" >> headers.txt
done < targets.txt
CVE SEARCH SEQUENCE
searchsploit <product> <exact_version>    # exact match first
searchsploit <product> <major.minor>      # broader range second
# Then: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/search  # authoritative CVSS + affected ranges
NUCLEI INTEGRATION
nuclei -u http://target -t http/technologies/ -silent   # version confirmation
nuclei -u http://target -t http/cves/ -silent           # CVE template checks
nuclei -u http://target -as -silent                     # auto scan, broader coverage
FALSE POSITIVE FILTER
[ ] Tier 1 confidence — exact version confirmed?
[ ] Version in affected range per CVE advisory?
[ ] Vulnerable feature or module confirmed enabled?
[ ] Behavioral verification passes?
FINDING FORMAT
Finding:      [Vulnerability name]
CVE:          [CVE-YYYY-XXXXX]
Evidence:     [Header value] — Tier [N], [confidence description]
Verification: [curl command] returned [result]
Severity:     [CVSS score with context]
